title: Killing not a racist act, father says
article: The father of teenager Keyvan Tabesh says his son was shot dead by a policeman in British Columbia who could not have known that his son was Iranian.

"My son had blue eyes. He had a European face, like he was from England or Spain, not Iran. This is not racist," Keyvan Tabesh's father, Nasser, said yesterday in an interview. "The bullet that shot into my son's heart was shot at a Canadian teenager, not at someone from Iran."

This week, the Iranian government tried to draw a parallel between the fatal shooting of Mr. Tabesh, 18, on July 14 in the Vancouver suburb of Port Moody and the death of Montreal photojournalist Zahra Kazemi in police custody on July 10 in Tehran.
Hamid Reza Asefi, a spokesman for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, was quoted as accusing Canadian police of "attacking" Iranian nationals in Vancouver.

Nasser Tabesh, a general surgeon in Iran for almost 30 years before the family moved to Canada three years ago, said he knew nothing about the exchange of accusations between the Iranian and Canadian governments.
"That's something between the two countries. [Iran] wants to use my son's death for their own purposes. . . . I have no idea about these things. I do not know anything about it."
No one from either the Canadian or Iranian government has spoken to him since his son's death last week, he also said.
"We're not a political family." The family was busy with their lives in Iran and stayed away from politics, he said.
Keyvan Tabesh was shot by a policeman around 2 a.m. on July 14. Earlier, the teenager had allegedly struck at a vehicle with a machete in an apparent road-rage incident, police have said.

The policeman, responding to a request on the police radio for help, cornered Mr. Tabesh in a cul-de-sac. The officer was in street clothes in a car with no police markings, no siren and no police lights. Police said Mr. Tabesh was shot when he ran at the officer's car waving the machete.
Dr. Tabesh said a passenger in his son's car who saw the shooting told the family that they did not know the man who trapped them was a police officer. They thought it was "a bad guy," he said.
Mr. Tabesh's body showed the impact of three bullets. His son was hit in his left shoulder, his left hand and his stomach, Dr. Tabesh said.
Amir Aghaei, who came to Vancouver from Tehran three years ago, was also shot.
He underwent an operation but still has the police bullet in his lower abdomen. He was released from hospital on July 19.
In his first interview since the incident, Mr. Aghaei said the policeman did not identify himself before he started shooting.
Although it was dark, they could see the face of the policeman in the car. "He was laughing at us, smiling . . . like a regular [person]."
They thought he was someone who lived on the street and who was playing with them. They had no way of knowing that he was a policeman, he added.
Mr. Tabesh got out of his car with the machete, to slam it against the side of the other vehicle to try to scare the person away. Mr. Aghaei also got out and tried to stop his friend, he said.
"The next thing I know, the guy gets out of his car, shouts 'Stop' and starts shooting. . . . Right away, he starts shooting."
Mr. Aghaei said the policeman had opened his car door and was shooting through the window, from behind the door. Mr. Aghaei was shot as he was running toward his friend.
"The next thing, that guy came to me. I said, 'Why did you shoot me, I was trying to help you."
"He said, 'I'm sorry sir, you were so close to me.' That's all he said."
The Port Moody Police Department has launched an investigation into the homicide and into how police handled the incident.
